findings.body:
getLoginPredicate now excludes org-linked non-public IDPs for all callers

getLoginPredicate() gained a clause excluding org-linked IDPs unless BROKER_PUBLIC=true. This predicate is reused by IdentityProviderBean.federatedProviderPredicate() to filter the user's already-linked (federated) identities on the login/account-linking pages. Previously a user's IDP linked to an organization (and not public) could appear there; now it will be filtered out. If that is not the intended behavior change for the federated-identities path, this silently hides legitimately-linked brokers. Please confirm this scope was intended, or restrict the new clause to the getForLogin caching path rather than the shared predicate.

remove() always does an extra DB lookup via getByAlias

remove() now unconditionally calls idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias) up front to support registerIDPLoginInvalidation. Previously the delegate lookup only happened in the isInvalid branch. This adds a storage round-trip to every IDP removal even when the entry is already cached (the else branch reads from cache). Consider reusing the cached CachedIdentityProvider model in the else branch for the login-invalidation check instead of always hitting the delegate, to avoid the regression on the common (cached) path.

findings.body:
Equal provider order silently picks one instead of failing

Previously, finding more than one CryptoProvider on the classpath threw an IllegalStateException to prevent accidental mixups (e.g. FIPS vs non-FIPS). Now providers are sorted by order() and the highest is silently chosen, only logging ignored ones at debug level. But DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order()==200, so when two of them are on the classpath the winner is decided by ServiceLoader iteration order (effectively arbitrary). A FIPS deployment that accidentally has the default provider on the classpath would now silently run with the wrong crypto provider instead of failing fast. Consider keeping a hard error (or at least a WARN) when multiple providers share the same highest order, and only allow the new behavior when one strictly outranks the others.

debugf called with dynamic string as format string

logger.debugf(builder.toString()) passes the constructed message as the format string. If any ignored provider class name ever contained a '%' it would be interpreted as a format specifier and could throw an IllegalFormatException / produce garbage. Use logger.debug(builder.toString()) (non-format variant) instead. Minor, but it is an avoidable format-string misuse.

readSequence mishandles indefinite-length encoding

readLength() may return -1 for indefinite-length (0x80) encoding. In readSequence the loop `while (length > 0)` then never executes and an empty list is returned silently for a malformed/indefinite sequence, rather than throwing. Since this decoder is only fed DER (definite length) signatures this is unlikely in practice, but for robustness readSequence should reject length < 0 (indefinite length) explicitly instead of returning an empty result. asn1derToConcatenatedRS would then fail with the clearer 'size different to 2' error, but a direct check here is preferable.

judgments.reasoning: The finding flags a real behavioral risk: when multiple CryptoProvider implementations have the same highest order, selection becomes dependent on ServiceLoader iteration order and may silently choose the wrong provider (e.g., non-FIPS in a FIPS deployment). This is not the same as golden[0], which is about returning the wrong provider in a specific keystore/BouncyCastle context, and golden[1] is unrelated dead code. The suggested fail-fast or warning on ties is a valid additional issue.

The finding points out a real potential misuse of debugf by passing an untrusted/dynamic string as the format, which could misinterpret '%' and cause formatting issues. This is not covered by the golden comments (wrong provider selection, dead ASN1Encoder code), so it’s a separate valid suggestion.
The finding flags the same dead-code issue described in golden comment [1]: two ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) calls whose results are discarded before the actual encoding in the return statement.

The finding points out a plausible correctness/robustness issue in ASN1Decoder: if readLength() can return -1 for indefinite-length encoding, readSequence() would silently return an empty list instead of rejecting unsupported/invalid input. This is not covered by the golden comments (which concern provider selection and dead code), and the suggested explicit rejection is a reasonable improvement.

findings.body:
RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE changed 4->3: breaking exit-code contract

The recreate-upgrade exit code is silently changed from 4 to 3, and 4 is reassigned to the new FEATURE_DISABLED case. The command exit codes are a documented public contract used by automation/DevOps pipelines (per update-compatibility.adoc). Any existing script that treats exit code 4 as 'recreate required' will now misinterpret it as 'feature disabled', and code 3 as a previously-unused/error value will now mean recreate. While the docs in this PR were updated to match, this is a backward-incompatible change to released behavior. Confirm this is acceptable (feature is preview) and call it out in release notes. Also note FEATURE_DISABLED lacks the _EXIT_CODE suffix used by the sibling constants, hurting consistency.

testFeatureNotEnabled does not assert the FEATURE_DISABLED exit code

The new test only asserts the error message but never verifies the exit code is FEATURE_DISABLED (4). The exit code is a documented contract and the most important observable behavior of the new feature-disabled path (CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED). Without asserting cliResult.exitCode() == 4, a regression in the exit code (e.g. accidentally returning 0 or colliding with the recreate code) would go undetected. Consider adding an exit-code assertion for both the metadata and check subcommands when the feature is disabled.

Null updateStrategy path skips enabling rolling-updates feature

createInitialDeployment returns early with 'return kc' when updateStrategy == null, before the new block that enables Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES on the FeatureSpec. If any parameterized case passes a null strategy and still exercises update/compatibility behavior that now requires the preview feature, the deployment will lack the feature and behave differently than the non-null cases. Verify the null-strategy case does not rely on update functionality; if it does, move the feature-enable block before the early return.

findings.body:
hasPermission missing resourceId filter, risk of over-granting via all-clients …

Unlike UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the scope-matching loop here does not filter by permission.getResourceId().equals(resource.getId()). When the per-client resource is absent and evaluation falls back to the all-clients resource, the returned permissions are matched solely by scope name. If a permission for the all-clients resource grants a scope (e.g. VIEW), a check for a different scope could still match across permissions if multiple permissions are returned for the resource set. To stay consistent with the user evaluator and avoid scope leakage between permissions, restrict matching to permissions whose resourceId equals the evaluated resource id. Please confirm the intended semantics and align with UserPermissionsV2.

Remove the unused method/imports to avoid confusion and reduce maintenance surface.

findings.body:
Anchor regex matches other tags like <abbr>, <address>

ANCHOR_PATTERN = "</?a[^>]*>" matches any tag whose name starts with 'a' because [^>]* greedily consumes the rest of the name. So <abbr>, <address>, <area> are treated as anchor tags by santizeAnchors. A translation containing e.g. <abbr> would be stripped/validated as an anchor and could either bypass the no-anchor sanitization or produce spurious "Didn't find anchor tag" errors. Anchor the tag name so only real <a> tags match.

Proposed patch:
```diff
--- a/misc/theme-verifier/src/main/java/org/keycloak/themeverifier/VerifyMessageProperties.java
+++ b/misc/theme-verifier/src/main/java/org/keycloak/themeverifier/VerifyMessageProperties.java
@@ -130,3 +130,3 @@
-    private static final Pattern ANCHOR_PATTERN = Pattern.compile("</?a[^>]*>");
+    private static final Pattern ANCHOR_PATTERN = Pattern.compile("</?a(\\s[^>]*)?>");
 
     /**
```

Missing English base file throws unchecked RuntimeException

verifySafeHtml derives the English source file by string-replacement and opens it with FileInputStream, throwing a raw RuntimeException if it is missing. verify() only catches IOException, so this RuntimeException escapes as an unchecked exception rather than a MojoExecutionException, crashing the build instead of reporting a verifier message. Community translations may exist for keys/files whose '_en' base does not exist in the resources tree (the path derivation also only swaps 'resources-community'->'resources'), so a missing English file is plausible and should be handled gracefully (e.g. treat as empty English bundle or wrap in MojoExecutionException).

Unintended range in English-file regex character class

The replacement regex "_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties" contains [a-zA-Z-_]; the '-' between 'Z' and '_' is interpreted as a range Z-_ (code points 90..95), which additionally matches '[', '\\', ']', '^', '`'. While unlikely to cause harm for normal locale suffixes, the character class is almost certainly not what was intended. Escape or reposition the hyphen, e.g. [a-zA-Z_-] or [a-zA-Z\\-_].

santizeAnchors removes wrong occurrence with replaceFirst

In santizeAnchors, when a matched anchor equals the corresponding English anchor, value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "") removes the FIRST occurrence of that anchor text anywhere in value, not the specific occurrence the matcher found. If value contains two identical anchor strings (e.g. two '<a href=...>' with the same attributes) but the surrounding text differs, the removal can delete an occurrence other than the validated one, and the loop's matcher (bound to the original string) keeps iterating. This can mis-validate translations with repeated identical anchors. Consider building the result via Matcher.appendReplacement/region-based removal instead of replaceFirst.

findings.body:
Dynamic shortcut refresh bypasses duplicate validation

postInit validates that no two grant types share a shortcut by comparing map sizes. But getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut lazily add newly-deployed grant factories to the maps at runtime without re-running that validation. If a dynamically deployed grant type returns a shortcut already used by another grant (e.g. an existing 'ac'/'rt' value), the put silently overwrites the existing grantsByShortcuts mapping, so getGrantTypeByShortcut will then decode previously-issued tokens to the wrong grant type. Consider validating uniqueness when adding entries lazily, or rejecting collisions instead of overwriting.

No null check on TokenContextEncoderProvider before use

initToken now calls session.getProvider(TokenContextEncoderProvider.class) and immediately dereferences it. If the SPI provider is not configured/available, getProvider returns null and token creation NPEs for every token issued. Since this is on the core token-issuance path, a missing provider takes down all token flows. Consider asserting non-null with a clear error, or a fallback to the previous plain generateId() behavior.

Removed copy-constructor may break external callers

The Context copy-constructor (Context(Context context)) was removed and replaced with a grantType field initialized from formParams. Removing a public constructor from an SPI type in server-spi-private is a backward-compatibility break for any subclass/extension relying on it. Also note grantType is now derived from formParams.getFirst(GRANT_TYPE) only in the main constructor; ensure all code paths that previously used the copy-constructor set formParams with the grant_type present, otherwise getGrantType() returns null and downstream encoding falls back to UNKNOWN.

Confirm all OAuth2GrantTypeFactory impls override getShortcut()

getShortcut() is added as an abstract method with no default. All in-tree factories were updated, but any third-party/external OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations will now fail to compile, and DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit will NPE/throw when iterating factories whose getShortcut() returns null (grantsByShortcuts.put(null,...) then size mismatch or null key issues). Consider providing a default method (e.g. derived from getId or a stable hash) to preserve compatibility.

getShouldUseLightweightToken depends on context client being set

AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken calls session.getContext().getClient().getAttribute(...). In getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext this is invoked during token id encoding; if the context client is not set at that point (some grant/token-exchange paths set client separately), getClient() returns null and this NPEs. Verify the context client is always populated before initToken runs for all grant flows touched by this PR.

findings.body:
Reader thread not joined: assertion races with in-flight reads

The reader thread is started but never joined. After the delete loop sets deletedAll=true, the main thread immediately runs `assertThat(caughtExceptions, empty())`. However the reader thread may still be executing an in-flight `groups()` request at that moment — precisely the read that overlaps the concurrent deletes the test is trying to validate. An exception thrown by that in-flight request gets added to `caughtExceptions` only AFTER the assertion has already passed, so the test can spuriously pass and miss the very regression it covers. It can also pass before any read overlaps the deletes at all. Capture the thread reference, set the flag, then `thread.join()` (with a timeout) BEFORE asserting, so all reads have completed and exceptions are collected.

findings.body:
Local cache poisons limit enforcement; device denied once then allowed

TagDevice now propagates errors (return err), and Authenticate denies auth on ErrDeviceLimitReached. But tagDeviceUI (impl.go ~line 87) calls a.localCache.SetDefault(key, ...) BEFORE a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. When CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the cache entry has already been set. The next request for the same device within the 29-min cache TTL hits the cache, returns nil, and the user is authenticated despite the limit. This makes enforcement non-deterministic: the same device is rejected on the first request but allowed on subsequent ones. Move SetDefault to after a successful CreateOrUpdateDevice so failed/limited tagging is not cached.

updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for stale known devices

updateDevice runs UPDATE ... WHERE device_id=? AND updated_at BETWEEN now-30d AND now+1m, and treats rowsAffected==0 as ErrDeviceLimitReached. This conflates two distinct cases: (a) an unknown/new device (correctly blocked), and (b) an existing, legitimate device whose updated_at is older than anonymousDeviceExpiration (30d). Case (b) — a returning user who was idle >30 days — gets ErrDeviceLimitReached and is denied authentication even though they are a previously known device, not a new one over the limit. Consider checking existence separately, or widening/removing the lower BETWEEN bound so known devices are always refreshed regardless of how stale their updated_at is.

Tagging moved to synchronous path adds DB latency/failure to auth

Previously TagDevice ran in a background goroutine with a 2-minute timeout and panic recovery, isolating tagging from the auth request. Now it runs synchronously inside Authenticate using the request ctx. This means every anonymous auth performs CountDevices + Create/Update DB queries on the hot path, and any non-limit DB error is only logged (good), but the removal of the recover() means a panic in TagDevice now propagates up through Authenticate. Also, the request-scoped ctx may be cancelled mid-write. Confirm this latency/cancellation tradeoff is intended; at minimum the lost panic-recovery guard around the DB call should be reconsidered.

anonymousDeviceLimit field typed implicitly as undefined

`anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` gives the property the inferred type `undefined` in some TS configs (the class field has no type annotation), whereas the interface declares `number | undefined`. While the interface implementation widens it, relying on the bare `undefined` initializer is fragile and the value is never populated from backend settings here. Verify the runtime actually copies anonymousDeviceLimit from the bootData/frontend settings JSON into GrafanaBootConfig; otherwise the frontend always sees undefined despite the backend sending it. An explicit `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;` annotation is clearer.

TOCTOU between CountDevices and insert allows exceeding device limit

CreateOrUpdateDevice checks CountDevices >= deviceLimit and, if under the limit, falls through to an INSERT/upsert. There is no transaction or unique-count enforcement spanning the count and the insert, so concurrent anonymous requests can each read count == limit-1 and all proceed to insert, pushing the actual device count above deviceLimit. Given tagging now runs synchronously per request, concurrent first-time devices can race past the cap. Consider performing the count and insert within a single transaction/locked section, or enforcing the limit at the DB level.

findings.body:
Denial cache short-circuits before allow cache, hiding fresh grants

The permDenialCache is consulted first and returns Allowed:false immediately for up to shortCacheTTL, before the permCache (allow) is even checked. There is no invalidation path: permCache/permDenialCache are TTL-only. If a user is denied for (action,name,parentFolder), then subsequently granted that permission, the next Check will still return deny for the remainder of the denial TTL even though the permCache may already hold the new allowing scope. This is a behavior regression: previously every Check re-evaluated permissions. Because authorization denials are now sticky, recently-granted access can be incorrectly rejected. Consider invalidating the denial cache when permissions are refreshed, or only caching denials with awareness that grants must clear them.

permissionCacheUsage metric records cache miss on a cache hit

In the cached-permissions branch, when getCachedIdentityPermissions succeeds (cache hit) but checkPermission returns allowed=false, the code falls through and unconditionally increments permissionCacheUsage("false") at line 137. This double-counts: the lookup WAS a cache hit, but it is reported as a miss. Only the allowed==true path increments "true". As a result, cache-hit-but-denied checks pollute the miss metric and the cache hit-rate is understated. Move the "false" increment into an explicit cache-miss (err != nil) branch.

Denial cache key can collide with permission cache key (shared backing store)

All cacheWrap instances share the same underlying cache.Cache, so keys live in one namespace. userPermDenialCacheKey produces namespace+".perm_"+uid+"_"+action+"_"+name+"_"+parent, while userPermCacheKey produces namespace+".perm_"+uid+"_"+action. Since action/name/parent are concatenated with "_" and may themselves contain underscores, a perm key for action "a_dash1_fold1" collides with a denial key for action "a", name "dash1", parent "fold1". A bool denial value would then be read by permCache.Get and fail to unmarshal into map[string]bool (degrading to a cache miss), or vice versa. Use a distinct prefix for the denial cache (e.g. ".permdenial_") to eliminate the ambiguity.

getCachedIdentityPermissions returns nil map on hit-miss without distinguishing…

For TypeRenderService the function always returns cache.ErrNotFound, forcing a full DB fallback on every render-service Check/List. That is acceptable, but combined with the new permDenialCache write in Check, a render service that is denied will get its denial cached under its UserUID even though its permissions are never cacheable as allows, making render-service denials sticky for shortCacheTTL while allows are always recomputed. Confirm render-service identities should participate in the denial cache, or skip denial caching for identity types whose permissions are not cached.

No test covers denial-cache staleness after a subsequent grant

TestService_CacheCheck covers allow-from-cache, fallback, outdated cache, and an explicit deny entry, but there is no regression test asserting behavior when a denial is cached and the user is later granted access (the staleness case). Given the new sticky-denial behavior, a test that sets a denial entry and then a permitting permCache entry, and asserts the intended result, would lock in the contract and catch future changes to invalidation logic.

In-process client switched to NoopCache

ProvideAuthZClient now wraps the in-process server with authzlib.NewClient using NoopCache, removing the client-side local cache that the remote path still uses. This relies entirely on the new service-level caching in rbac/service.go. Verify the in-process path actually benefits from the service-level cache (the service caches permissions, but the authlib client previously cached full Check/List decisions). Removing decision-level caching here may increase per-request work for in-proc deployments.

LoggerMiddleware now silently depends on ContextualLoggerMiddleware for context…

The refactor removed pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID, uname and traceID from logParams and instead relies on `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)` to recover them. Those attributes only end up in the context if NewContextualLoggerMiddleware ran earlier in the chain (it injects them via log.WithContextualAttributes), and traceID only if the tracing service registered its contextual provider. This creates an implicit ordering/coupling dependency: if LoggerMiddleware is ever used without ContextualLoggerMiddleware preceding it (e.g. a different middleware assembly, tests, or reordering), the 'Plugin Request Completed' log silently loses all plugin/datasource/user/trace identification, regressing observability with no compile-time guarantee. Consider documenting the required ordering or keeping a minimal fallback (at least pluginId/endpoint) in logRequest.

Plugin request skipped entirely when plugin not registered

instrumentPluginRequest (and instrumentPluginRequestSize) call pluginTarget first and return early with ErrPluginNotRegistered if the plugin is not in the registry, meaning fn(ctx) (the actual downstream call) is never executed and QueryData/CallResource return nil response + that error. Because this metrics middleware sits near the top of the chain (before LoggerMiddleware/auth/etc.), any transient registry inconsistency makes the whole request fail rather than just losing a metric label. If this behavior was inherited from the previous instrumentation middleware it is at least preserved, but it is worth confirming the registry is always populated before requests reach here; otherwise a failed target lookup should degrade gracefully (use an 'unknown' target and still run fn) instead of aborting the request.

NewMetricsMiddleware shares one mutable instance; next overwritten on re-wrap

newMetricsMiddleware builds a single *MetricsMiddleware, and the returned ClientMiddlewareFunc closure mutates `imw.next = next` on that shared instance each time it is applied. If the middleware factory's resulting ClientMiddleware is applied to more than one client (or the chain is assembled more than once from the same factory value), all instances share state and the last assignment to `next` wins, corrupting earlier chains. The same instance is also not safe if wrapped concurrently. Prefer constructing a fresh MetricsMiddleware (copying the pluginMetrics/registry) inside the closure, or document that the factory must be applied exactly once.

FromContext fallback uses New() instead of returning self

When d.l.FromContext(ctx) does not type-assert to *log.ConcreteLogger, the wrapper returns d.New(), which creates a brand-new child logger (via d.l.New()) and discards any context-derived attributes. In the infra implementation FromContext returns the same *ConcreteLogger when there are no contextual args, so the assertion normally succeeds; but if the underlying implementation ever returns a different Logger type, callers silently lose the contextual logger AND get an unnecessarily re-derived child. Returning a wrapper around d.l (i.e. `return d` / `&grafanaInfraLogWrapper{l: d.l}`) would be a safer fallback than New().

FromContext added to Logger interface

FromContext is a new method on the exported Logger interface. Any external/third-party implementer of plugins/log.Logger will fail to compile until they add FromContext, so this is a breaking interface change. The in-repo implementations (grafanaInfraLogWrapper, TestLogger) are updated, but confirm there are no other implementers (including in dependent modules) before merge.

TestLogger.FromContext discards captured-log state

FromContext returns NewTestLogger(), a fresh TestLogger, instead of the receiver f. Tests that obtain a logger, call FromContext(ctx), then log and later assert on the original instance's DebugLogs/InfoLogs/etc. will see no captured output because the logging went to the discarded new instance. If any test relies on inspecting logs emitted after a FromContext call this will silently break the assertion; returning f (or a clone that shares the capture fields) would preserve observability.

findings.body:
Eager Init in constructor blocks startup on full index build

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously, which invokes s.search.init(ctx). That builds every resource index from scratch (errgroup over GetResourceStats, full ListIterator per namespace) before the constructor returns. Previously init was lazy (sync.Once on first request). This turns server construction into a potentially long, blocking operation and makes any transient init failure (e.g. backend not ready) fatal to creation with no retry, since sync.Once permanently caches initErr. Callers in client.go/restoptions.go/service.go construct the server during wiring; a slow or failing index build now blocks/aborts startup. Consider keeping index build asynchronous or making constructor-time init failures non-fatal/retryable.

History/Origin can nil-deref when search is not configured

The s.Init(ctx) guard was removed from History and Origin, and neither checks s.search for nil before calling s.search.History/Origin. When opts.Search.Resources == nil, newSearchSupport returns nil and s.search stays nil (Search() guards this with an explicit nil check, but History/Origin do not). A call to History or Origin on a server without search configured will panic with a nil pointer dereference. Add the same `if s.search == nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("search index not configured") }` guard used in Search().

cacheMu no longer serializes concurrent BuildIndex for same key

BuildIndex previously held cacheMu.Lock() for its whole duration; now the lock only wraps the final cache map write. Combined with search.init() running builds concurrently via errgroup, two concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key can both create a bleve index (and a file-backed dir at the same path via bleve.New) and both write to the cache, with the later overwriting the earlier. The earlier index returned to its caller then diverges from the cached one, and concurrent file-index creation on the same directory may error or corrupt. The original lock prevented duplicate same-key builds. If parallelism across keys is the goal, use a per-key lock rather than dropping the build-time exclusion entirely.

This PR changes server initialization to run eagerly in the constructor (full index build), yet the only integration test exercising the storage server target is now skipped for postgres with a comment that it 'works locally' but not in Drone. findings.body:
close() drops final offset commits, causing reprocessing on restart

close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread (which then stops running), and only afterwards calls queue_pool.shutdown() which drains remaining queued work items and marks their offsets complete. No commit pass runs after the drain, so all offsets for items processed during shutdown are never committed. On restart those messages are reprocessed. Arroyo expects close()/join() to flush pending commits. Add a final get_committable_offsets()/commit_function() pass after queue_pool.shutdown().

Proposed patch:
```diff
--- a/src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py
+++ b/src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py
@@ -335,6 +335,11 @@
     def close(self) -> None:
         self.shutdown_event.set()
         self.commit_thread.join(timeout=5.0)
         self.queue_pool.shutdown()
+        # Workers may have completed offsets during the final drain above; perform
+        # one last commit pass so those offsets are not reprocessed on restart.
+        committable = self.queue_pool.offset_tracker.get_committable_offsets()
+        if committable:
+            self.commit_function(committable)
 
     def terminate(self) -> None:
         self.shutdown_event.set()

```

Worker commits offset even when result_processor raises (silent data loss)

In OrderedQueueWorker.run, an exception from result_processor is caught and only logged, then the finally block calls complete_offset(). This marks the offset as successfully processed, so the commit loop advances past it. A transient failure (e.g. DB outage) therefore results in the message being permanently skipped rather than retried — silent data loss. Other modes rely on RunTask/arroyo retry semantics. Consider not completing the offset (or re-raising to trigger backpressure/retry) when processing fails, or at minimum make this drop-on-error behavior an explicit, documented decision. Note tests/sentry/uptime/.../test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling assumes the offset is NOT committed on error, contradicting this code.

Double queue_pool.shutdown(): factory.shutdown vs strategy.close

ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() now calls self.queue_pool.shutdown() and sets queue_pool = None. But SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() also calls self.queue_pool.shutdown() on the same pool instance (the strategy holds its own reference). Depending on arroyo lifecycle ordering, shutdown() runs on an already-shut-down pool: queue.shutdown() is re-invoked (caught) and worker.join() is called again. More importantly, whichever path runs second sees an already-drained pool, so the final-commit logic must live wherever the pool is actually drained. Confirm only one component owns pool shutdown/commit-flush to avoid lost final commits and redundant joins.

get_committable_offsets is O(offset range); large gaps cause long scans

get_committable_offsets iterates range(start, max_offset + 1) for each partition every second. If a low offset stays outstanding (slow/stuck worker) while higher offsets keep arriving, max_offset grows unbounded relative to start and all_offsets accumulates (mark_committed only prunes on successful commit). The linear scan and growing set are then repeated each second, degrading throughput and memory under a single slow group. Consider tracking the contiguous frontier incrementally or bounding the scan to known tracked offsets instead of the full integer range.

async forEach swallows getCalendar/deleteEvent errors and doesn't await

getCalendar is now async, so the forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...) callback returns a promise that nothing awaits. The surrounding try/catch can no longer catch rejections from getCalendar() or deleteEvent()/deleteMeeting() — they become unhandled promise rejections, and Reschedule() proceeds (sending emails, etc.) before the calendar/video events are actually deleted. Previously getCalendar was synchronous so errors threw inside forEach and were caught. Convert to awaited iteration, e.g. `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))`, so deletions complete and errors are caught. Note: a plain for...of with the existing `return` statements would early-return out of Reschedule, so use map+Promise.all rather than a bare loop.

But the recurring branch here was left as `.forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(...) })`. Because forEach does not await the async callbacks, the outer function continues and apiDeletes is awaited before these pushes happen, so recurring-booking calendar events may never be deleted and errors are swallowed. Inverted condition for organization slug assignment

The original code set `slug` only when team billing was disabled: `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })`. The refactor changed it to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, inverting the condition. Now `slug` is set only when billing IS enabled, while `requestedSlug` is also set in the same enabled case. The result: with billing enabled both slug and requestedSlug are written; with billing disabled neither is written, so a newly created org has no slug. This contradicts the prior behavior where billing-disabled orgs got a slug directly and billing-enabled orgs got a requestedSlug pending approval.

Proposed patch:

```diff
--- a/packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/organizations/create.handler.ts
+++ b/packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/organizations/create.handler.ts
@@ -148,9 +148,9 @@ export const createHandler = async ({ input, ctx }: CreateOptions) => {
         organization: {
           create: {
             name,
-            ...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {}),
+            ...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {}),
             metadata: {
               ...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { requestedSlug: slug } : {}),
               isOrganization: true,
               isOrganizationVerified: false,
               isOrganizationConfigured,

```

Broken destinationCalendar fallback in updateEvent/deleteEvent

In both updateEvent (line ~255) and deleteEvent (line ~315) the fallback branch is `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. This branch only executes when `externalCalendarId` is falsy (undefined/empty), so the `find` is searching for a calendar whose `externalId === undefined`, which never matches a real entry and always yields `undefined`. The original logic used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` (the destination's own externalId). With the array refactor this should select the relevant destination calendar (e.g. the first / matching credential), not compare against the empty `externalCalendarId`. As written the fallback is dead, so updates/deletes silently fall back to `defaultCalendarId`/primary instead of the configured destination calendar.

Team destination calendars dropped when no primary destination calendar

evt.destinationCalendar is built as `[eventType.destinationCalendar]`, else `[organizerUser.destinationCalendar]`, else `null`. For a COLLECTIVE team event where neither the eventType nor the organizer has a destinationCalendar, `evt.destinationCalendar` is `null`. The subsequent `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` then silently no-ops due to optional chaining, so all collected team member destination calendars are discarded and their calendar events are never created. Initialize the array (e.g. to `[]`) before pushing, or push into a guaranteed array.

The refactored dynamic-booking branch (`!eventTypeId`) removed the `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` from the user `select` that existed before. Downstream the user objects are typed/treated as `IsFixedAwareUser` which declares `organization: { slug: string }`, and organization slug is relied upon elsewhere for org-scoped users. Omitting it means dynamic bookings for organization users lose org context (slug becomes undefined), which can break org credential/branding/url resolution. Inside the recurring-event branch, the inner promise loop builds deletions across all updatedBookings for EACH outer reference, so with multiple calendar references the same recurring events may be deleted multiple times (duplicate deleteEvent calls). findings.body:
Public options type drops discriminated-union safety (silent NOTHING)

InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions widens scope to a plain string union and makes teamId optional. The constructor validates options with the discriminated-union zod schema and, on failure, silently sets this.options = null, which makes buildAuthorizationConditions return NOTHING_CONDITION (1=0). Previously the constructor accepted InsightsBookingServiceOptions (the discriminated union), so a caller passing scope:'team' without teamId, or an invalid scope, was caught at compile time. Now such mistakes compile fine and degrade at runtime to an empty result set with no error, which is hard to diagnose and can mask authorization-config bugs. Consider keeping the discriminated union for the constructor parameter type, or surfacing a validation error instead of silently nulling options.

Caching tests removed but caching logic still present

The entire "Caching" describe block (tests for cached authorization and filter conditions) was deleted. However getAuthorizationConditions/getFilterConditions still implement the cachedAuthConditions / cachedFilterConditions memoization, including the subtle cachedFilterConditions === undefined vs null distinction (null is a valid cached value meaning 'no filters'). With the tests gone, a regression where null caching breaks (e.g. re-running buildFilterConditions on every call, or treating null as uncached) would no longer be caught. Recommend restoring equivalent caching coverage adapted to the new Prisma.Sql return type.

getBaseConditions: unreachable NOTHING branch; authConditions always truthy

In getBaseConditions, authConditions is the result of getAuthorizationConditions which always returns a Prisma.Sql object (NOTHING_CONDITION when unauthorized), never null/undefined. Since a Prisma.Sql is always truthy, the `else if (filterConditions)` and final `else { return NOTHING_CONDITION }` branches are dead code. More importantly, the truthiness checks suggest an intent for authConditions to possibly be empty/absent, which it never is. This is functionally safe (unauthorized still yields 1=0 AND filters), but the branching is misleading. Consider simplifying to: if filterConditions return (auth) AND (filter), else return auth.

org scope: org-level members missed when org has no child teams

buildOrgAuthorizationCondition computes userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0. teamIds always includes options.orgId, so memberships attached directly to the org entity exist but are skipped whenever the org has no child teams, producing an auth condition that omits the isTeamBooking=false user clause. This logic is carried over from the prior implementation, but the rewrite is a good opportunity to fix it: guard on teamIds.length (always > 0) rather than teamsFromOrg.length, so org-level members are always included. If intentional, please document why org-direct members are excluded.

try/catch cannot catch errors from fire-and-forget async deletes

deleteScheduledEmailReminder/deleteScheduledSMSReminder are async and are invoked inside forEach without await. The surrounding try/catch only catches synchronous throws; rejected promises from these calls escape the catch and become unhandled rejections. Either await the deletions (e.g. via Promise.all over a map) or rely on the internal try/catch in the managers and drop the misleading wrapper.

One failed SendGrid cancel aborts the entire cancellation batch

The cancel loop awaits client.request() sequentially inside a single try block, then collects deletes and runs Promise.all afterward. If any SendGrid cancel throws (already-sent batch, network error), the catch aborts the loop: remaining cancelled reminders are skipped this run, and reminders already cancelled in SendGrid never get their workflowReminder.delete() executed (Promise.all is never reached). They linger with cancelled:true and are retried each cron tick. Wrap each iteration's request in its own try/catch (or Promise.allSettled) so a single failure doesn't block the rest, and delete each row right after a successful cancel.

immediateDelete branch leaves WorkflowReminder row undeleted

When immediateDelete is true, the function cancels the SendGrid send and returns without deleting the WorkflowReminder row. This relies on every caller separately cascade-deleting the row (workflow/step deletion paths do). It's an implicit contract that's easy to violate (see handleNewBooking reschedule). Consider deleting the row in the immediateDelete branch too (like deleteScheduledSMSReminder always does) so the function is self-consistent and callers don't leak rows.

Prisma and PrismaPromise are moved from `import type` to the value import. PrismaPromise and Prisma (used only as a type namespace, e.g. Prisma.BatchPayload) are types; importing them as values is unnecessary and, under isolatedModules/verbatimModuleSyntax, PrismaPromise as a value can fail since it has no runtime export. Keep them in a separate `import type`.

findings.body:
minimumTokenResponseSchema is built incorrectly with computed keys

The object literal uses computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. These evaluate to fixed literal strings (the result of calling `.toString()` on a ZodString instance, e.g. "[object Object]"), so they produce one or two bogus fixed property names mapped to `z.number()`/`z.unknown()`. This is NOT a passthrough/catchall — extra token fields (like `expiry_date`, `expires_in`) are dropped by `z.object`, and the literal keys will almost never match real response keys, so `safeParse` will strip everything except `access_token`. The intent (allow arbitrary extra properties, treat numeric props as expiry) is not achieved. Use `z.object({ access_token: z.string() }).catchall(z.unknown())` (or `.passthrough()`) instead.

Salesforce connection uses stale access_token after refresh

After successfully refreshing the token via the new fetch and persisting `accessTokenParsed.data` to the DB, the returned `jsforce.Connection` is still created with the OLD `credentialKey.access_token` (and old instanceUrl), not the freshly refreshed token. This defeats the purpose of refreshing: the connection will use an expired/stale access token. Use `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token` (and the refreshed instance_url) for the connection.

Proposed patch:
```diff
--- a/packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts
+++ b/packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts
@@ -104,5 +104,5 @@
       instanceUrl: credentialKey.instance_url,
-      accessToken: credentialKey.access_token,
+      accessToken: accessTokenParsed.data.access_token,
       refreshToken: credentialKey.refresh_token,
     });
   };

```

Fragile success check via response.statusText !== "OK"

`if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw ...` is unreliable. Under HTTP/2 (and many fetch implementations) `response.statusText` is an empty string even on success, which would make this throw on every successful refresh. Even on HTTP/1.1 the reason phrase is not guaranteed. Use `if (!response.ok)` instead to check the 2xx status range. Additionally, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` already throws on a failed parse, so the subsequent `if (!accessTokenParsed.success)` block is dead code — the function never returns an unsuccessful result.

Unhandled parse/decrypt errors return 500 and method not restricted

`appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a ZodError on malformed input, and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` throws on bad ciphertext/key — both surface as an unhandled 500 with a stack trace rather than a 400. There is also no HTTP method check, so a GET (with empty body) hits the same path. Consider using `safeParse` and try/catch around decrypt to return 400, and restrict to POST. Also note the webhook-secret comparison relies on a non-constant-time `!==`, which is a minor timing-leak concern for a shared secret.

Sync endpoint response not validated and request lacks auth/error handling

When `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is used, the fetch sends no authentication header (e.g. the webhook secret) and does not check `response.ok` — a non-2xx response is returned as-is to callers that then `.json()`/parse it, producing confusing downstream errors instead of a clear failure. The function also returns the raw `Response` for the sync path but the `refreshFunction()` result (often already-parsed data, e.g. axios/jsforce responses) for the fallback path, so callers receive inconsistent shapes. Consider validating `response.ok` and documenting/normalizing the return type.

refreshOAuthTokens return shape differs between sync and fallback paths

`refreshOAuthTokens` returns the value of `refreshFunction()` in the fallback path (here the hubspot SDK's `HubspotToken` object) but returns a raw `fetch` `Response` in the credential-sync path. The same inconsistency affects zoho-bigin (axios response vs Response) and other adapters that don't re-parse. The sync path needs to parse/normalize the response into the expected token shape.

findings.body:
Reminders failing to schedule deleted regardless of due date

The retryCount>1 delete branch is independent of scheduledDate. A reminder whose retryCount exceeds 1 (after 2 failed attempts) is deleted even if its scheduledDate is still days in the future. Combined with the fetch window (`scheduledDate lte now()+7d`), a reminder for an event 6 days away that hits 2 transient Twilio failures is permanently dropped and will never be retried closer to the event, when the transient condition may have cleared. Consider only deleting past-due reminders, or capping retries only for reminders that are actually due soon.

Retry increment skipped when message empty or sendTo missing

In the success path, retryCount is only incremented inside `if (message?.length && sendTo)` when `scheduledSMS` is falsy. If `message` is empty/null or `sendTo` is missing, the whole block is skipped: scheduled stays false and retryCount is never incremented, so the reminder is fetched again every cron run forever (never reaching retryCount>1 to be cleaned up). Such permanently-unsendable reminders (e.g. missing phone number) accumulate and are re-processed indefinitely. Consider incrementing retryCount or marking the reminder when it cannot be sent.

Assuming the described branch exists, it’s a distinct, plausible correctness concern.

findings.body:
Auth check uses && instead of ||, denying team ADMINs

`isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed with `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`. A membership has a single role, so this AND can only be true for an OWNER (who satisfies both isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner). A plain ADMIN passes isTeamAdmin but fails isTeamOwner, so the AND is false and the admin is wrongly forbidden — contradicting the variable's name and intent ("Admin OR Owner"). Note isTeamAdmin already returns truthy for both ADMIN and OWNER roles. Use `||`.

Proposed patch:
```diff
--- a/packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts
+++ b/packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts
@@ -46,4 +46,4 @@ export const addGuestsHandler = async ({ ctx, input }: AddGuestsOptions) => {
   const isTeamAdminOrOwner =
-    (await isTeamAdmin(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0)) &&
+    (await isTeamAdmin(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0)) ||
     (await isTeamOwner(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0));
 

```

Blacklist comparison is case-sensitive against lowercased list

`blacklistedGuestEmails` is normalized to lowercase, but the incoming `guest` value is compared as-is via `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`. A guest email containing any uppercase characters (e.g. `Banned@Example.com`) will not match a lowercased blacklist entry, so the blacklist can be bypassed. Lowercase the guest before comparison.

Proposed patch:
```diff
--- a/packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts
+++ b/packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts
@@ -77,3 +77,3 @@ export const addGuestsHandler = async ({ ctx, input }: AddGuestsOptions) => {
       !booking.attendees.some((attendee) => guest === attendee.email) &&
-      !blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)
+      !blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest.toLowerCase())
   );

```

Organizer email subject can throw on empty attendees list

The subject interpolates `this.calEvent.attendees[0].name`. If `calEvent.attendees` is empty, this throws a TypeError when building the email payload. While the add-guests flow typically has attendees, the original booking could in edge cases have no attendees array populated for the cal event, and other organizer emails guard this. Consider `this.calEvent.attendees[0]?.name` or a fallback to organizer/team name.

handleAdd silently no-ops and lacks invalid-email reset

If all email rows are removed (`multiEmailValue.length === 0`) handleAdd returns with no user feedback. Also `isInvalidEmail` is set on failure but never reset when the user subsequently fixes the input and the validation passes only on a later attempt — once true it stays shown until the dialog is reopened/cancelled. Consider resetting `setIsInvalidEmail(false)` on a successful parse and providing feedback for the empty case.

No uniqueness/non-empty guard server-side

The server schema accepts any array of valid emails, including an empty array and duplicate addresses. The client enforces uniqueness, but the tRPC endpoint is callable directly. An empty `guests` array would pass validation and reach the handler (where uniqueGuests becomes empty -> BAD_REQUEST, acceptable), but duplicates within the input are only partially handled. Consider mirroring the client's uniqueness refine here for defense in depth.

sendAddGuestsEmails passes raw guests instead of added guests

The handler calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` with the raw input list rather than `uniqueGuests` (the ones actually added). Here `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` decides whether an attendee gets the full AttendeeScheduledEmail vs the AttendeeAddGuestsEmail notification. Since blacklisted/duplicate emails are not added to evt.attendees this is currently harmless, but it is fragile — if any filtered email coincidentally matches an existing attendee email, that pre-existing attendee would receive the wrong (scheduled) email. Pass the actually-added guest list.

findings.body:
sed -i '' is BSD/macOS-only and breaks on Linux

`sed -i '' -E ...` uses the BSD/macOS in-place syntax where '' is the backup suffix. On Linux (GNU sed) this treats '' as the script/expression argument and fails (or worse, misinterprets args), so the script cannot update GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL in CI/Linux dev environments. Since GNU and BSD sed in-place flags are incompatible, consider a portable approach (e.g. write to a temp file and mv, or detect the OS) rather than hardcoding the BSD form.

actions wrapper always renders, leaving empty w-32 div when dropdown is null

Previously `actions` was conditionally rendered only when a disconnect was allowed. Now the `<div className="flex w-32 justify-end">` wrapper is always rendered, and `CredentialActionsDropdown` returns `null` when `!canDisconnect && !hasCache` (e.g. delegation credentials with no cache). This leaves an empty 32-width spacer reserved in the layout for cards that previously had none, shifting alignment. Consider returning the wrapper conditionally or letting the dropdown's null result collapse the space.

Team-level credentials (userId null) cannot have cache cleared

The lookup filters `where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id }`. Team credentials have a null userId and a teamId instead, so for those the handler always throws "Credential not found", making the Delete-cache action silently fail for team/managed calendar credentials even when the user is a team admin. If the dropdown is shown for team credentials, this is a functional gap; consider also allowing access via team membership/admin checks (mirroring how credentials.delete authorizes).

Verify updateMany with empty data bumps updatedAt

`updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` relies on Prisma refreshing `@updatedAt` even with an empty `data` object. This is the core mechanism that powers cacheUpdatedAt/cache-status display. Prisma does set @updatedAt on updateMany with empty data, but this is subtle and easily broken by ORM upgrades. Consider passing an explicit field (or adding a test) so the behavior is intentional and not silently dependent on Prisma internals.
